2: A father, angry, shouted at his son: I give you to Death. So the boy, Nachiketa, went. Death wasn't home. The boy waited three days. To make up for it, Death offered him three wishes. For the last one, the boy asked: what happens when we die? Death offered him gold, horses, kingdoms instead. The boy said no. All of that ends. He wanted the one thing that doesn't. So Death gave him one word: om. One sound for everything, the part of everything that never ends. That's why Hindus start every prayer with om. Name the big thing first. Then ask for the small things.
3: A king rode up with his army to a sage's forest home. The sage fed every soldier, with a wonder cow that could give anything. The king wanted her. The sage said no. So the king tried to take her by force. And his whole army lost, to one old man with a staff. The king gave up his throne. After years of practice, he became a great sage himself: Vishvamitra. And the prayer he's remembered for doesn't ask for power, or to win. The Gayatri, the prayer millions of Hindus say every morning, asks for one thing. A clear mind. Before a big test, it doesn't ask for the grade. It asks to see straight.
4: The morning of the great war. Two armies of cousins, face to face. Then the eldest prince, Yudhishthira, takes off his armor, puts down his weapons, and walks alone toward the enemy. Everyone thinks he's surrendering. He isn't. He bows at the feet of his great-uncle and his teacher, the men about to fight him, and asks for their blessing. And they give it. Because a bow isn't about which side you're on. It's to what's sacred in a person. That's namaste. Namas: a bow. Te: to you. The light in me sees the light in you.
5: The gods won a great battle, and got proud. We did this. Then a strange being appeared. Agni, the god of fire, stepped up: I can burn anything on earth. The being set down a single blade of grass. Burn this. Agni threw everything he had at it. Nothing. He couldn't burn it. Then the being vanished, and a goddess told them: your power was never yours. It was borrowed, from the source of everything. That's why Hindus wave a flame in arti. It's light, offered back to where light comes from. Your wins are borrowed light too. Offer them back. Then share them.
6: In a king's court, a scholar pushed a sage: how many gods are there? Three thousand three hundred and six. Yes, but how many, really? Thirty-three. Really? Six. Three. Two. One and a half. Really? One. All the gods are faces of that one. An old verse says it in five words: truth is one, the wise call it by many names. So Hindus can love many gods, and still mean one. And most have one face of God that feels like home. That one is yours.
7: A robber held up travelers to feed his family. One day he stopped a sage, who asked him one question. Will your family share the weight of what you do? The robber ran home and asked. They said no. It was all his. His deeds were his alone. And so were the next ones. So the sage gave him a name of God to repeat. He sat so still, ants built a hill over him. He rose as Valmiki, the poet who wrote the Ramayana. That's karma. Not payback. Action. What you do, you become.
